| [LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md) | What Is It Like to Be a Bat? | Nagel (1974), [DOI-10.2307/2183914](https://doi.org/10.2307/2183914). An organism has conscious states if and only if there is something it is like to be that organism. That subjective character belongs to a type of point of view, and it is left out by every functional, intentional or causal analysis, since each is compatible with its absence. Reduction elsewhere moves away from a point of view toward the objective; here that move leads away from the thing being explained. So physicalism may be true, but we have no conception of how it could be. The paper argues, with no new theorem, that the Lombardi–da Costa ontology of properties for quantum mechanics can be stated in Krause's quasi-set theory Q. | [LIT-122](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-122.md) v2 | The Representation of Time and Change in Mechanics | Belot (2005), DOI-10.1016/B978-044451560-5/50005-1. For theories with ideal existence, uniqueness and a dynamical time-translation group, time is three intertwined ℝ-actions (on spacetime, on the symplectic space of solutions, and on the isomorphic space of initial data), and change is a slicing-indexed family of functions on those spaces. Singular dynamics, gauge freedom and time-dependence each damage this picture in a repairable way. Spatially compact vacuum GR breaks it, because the reduced Hamiltonian vanishes (h ≡ 0) and there is only one canonical isomorphism between the reduced spaces. That is the problem of time. It is not an artefact of the 3+1 split, it does not show change to be illusory, and it is absent from asymptotically flat GR and from artificially generally covariant theories. A parameterized "geometric time", such as CMC, restores change and, in the CMC case, a time-dependent Hamiltonian flow. | Active — read in full 2026-09-26 ([NOTE-118](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-118.md)); worth reading as the careful technical-philosophical statement of what the problem of time is and is not in classical GR. | [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md) v2 | Personal Identity and Ethics | Dufner (2025), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/identity-ethics/>. A survey, arguing no thesis of its own, of how three contested questions bear on ethics: which account of persistence is true (unique psychological continuity, Shoemaker and Parfit; or biological continuity and animalism, Olson and DeGrazia), whether identity or the psychological relations (continuity and/or connectedness) is what matters (Parfit's fission case), and whether metaphysics constrains ethics or the reverse. The book's thesis is that every viable theory of how consciousness fits into the cosmos, and of the cosmos's basic structure, is both "bizarre" (contrary to common sense) and "dubious" (not rationally compelling). So "something that seems almost too crazy to believe must be true" (p. 4), and credence should be spread across the bizarre options. Examples of those options are that the United States is conscious (if materialism is true), that we are sims or Boltzmann brains (a 0.1–1% credence), that space is transcendentally ideal, that almost every act causes almost every future event, and that there is no fact about snail consciousness. Its basic objects are optimisation problems, above all games, which are "mathematical structures … whose relata are distinguished as such by the mathematical representations … just like quarks and bosons" (§3). Dennett uses the criterion, with the Game of Life's gliders and eaters as the stepping stone (pp. 37–42), to defend "mild realism" about beliefs. Velleman argues that the "standard story" of action (desire + belief cause an intention, which causes movement) leaves the agent out. It fails even when every causal link is normal: his example is an intention to end a friendship, formed and executed without him (p. 104). Frankfurt's hierarchical remedy cannot fix it either. Any mental item picked out without presupposing the agent's participation (a second-order desire, a Watsonian value, a "decisive commitment") is one the agent can be alienated from. The result is "nonreductive functionalism": organisation fixes experience with natural, not metaphysical, necessity. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-347](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-347.md)); worth reading as the full statement of the principle of organizational invariance and the fading- and dancing-qualia arguments for it. It covers silicon replacement and, by the paper's own §3 extension, a population of homunculi that implements a human's neural organisation. It does not cover a system whose organisation is merely similar in kind to a conscious one, so it does not license Schwitzgebel's step to the United States ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)). The conclusion is nomological, not metaphysical ("nonreductive functionalism"), and it is a plausibility argument by the author's own account. |
| [LIT-395](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-395.md) | The Combination Problem for Panpsychism | Chalmers (2016/2017), in Brüntrup & Jaskolla (eds), Panpsychism: Contemporary Perspectives, OUP, pp. 179–214. How could micro-experiences constitute a macro-subject? The problem splits into subject, quality and structure versions; each yields an argument against constitutive (Russellian) panpsychism, of which the subject-summing and structural mismatch arguments are the strongest. Emergent, autonomous and identity panpsychism avoid combination at a cost in mental causation or physics. Phenomenal bonding, quantum holism, small palettes and informational composition are judged most worth pursuing. No solution is offered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-358](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-358.md)), from the author's posted draft, not the published chapter; worth reading as the map of the combination problem: it splits the problem into subject, quality and structure versions (plus unity, boundary, awareness and grain), turns each into an argument, and sorts every response into emergent, autonomous, identity or combinatorial panpsychism. It solves nothing and says so. Its conclusions are judgements of promise ("phenomenal bonding or quantum holism", "principles of informational composition"), not results. For this record its value is that the subject-summing argument is James's argument against group minds, and that its footnote 7 objects to IIT's exclusion postulate on grounds that have nothing to do with groups. |
| [LIT-396](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-396.md) | Psychological Predicates | Putnam (1967), in Capitan & Merrill (eds.), Art, Mind, and Religion (Proceedings of the 1965 Oberlin Colloquium in Philosophy), University of Pittsburgh Press, pp. 37–48; reprinted as "The Nature of Mental States". It proposes, as an empirical hypothesis, that pain is a functional state of a whole organism, a state of a probabilistic automaton fixed by its machine table, rather than a brain state. Condition (3) of the hypothesis is the anti-nesting stipulation: no pain-feeler "possesses a decomposition into parts which separately possess Descriptions" of the pain-capable kind, introduced only "to rule out such 'organisms' (if they can count as such) as swarms of bees as single pain-feelers". | Deferred — not read in full: the original (Art, Mind, and Religion, pp. 37–48) is closed on JSTOR. The University of Pittsburgh's page images sit behind a bot challenge I could not pass, and the Internet Archive copy of the 1975 reprint is print-disabled only. What was read is MIT's 24.09x course excerpt of the 1975 reprint ("The Nature of Mental States"), recorded as a Skimmed reading in [NOTE-335](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-335.md). That excerpt carries the four-clause hypothesis verbatim, including the anti-nesting condition (3) and its one-sentence motive. |
| [LIT-397](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-397.md) | Facing Backwards on the Problem of Consciousness | Dennett (1996), Journal of Consciousness Studies 3(1):4–6, a reply to Chalmers's "Facing Up". The easy/hard split is "a major misdirector of attention, an illusion-generator". A vitalist could pose the same "hard problem" of life, and a neuroscientist who set perception aside as hard would have misdescribed vision. Chalmers's reason why consciousness is different repeats the claim. Subtract every function from one's own consciousness and nothing is left but a conviction. Positing experience as fundamental, like mass and charge, needs independent evidence, which is not given ("cutism"). | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-346](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-346.md)); worth reading as the three-page statement of the deflationary reply to the hard problem, and as the source of the vitalism, "Crock" and "cutism" analogies. Its one argued point is a challenge, not a refutation: Chalmers owes independent evidence for experience as a fundamental property, the way physics has for mass and charge, and without it the posit does no explanatory work. Its central premise, that once every function is subtracted from one's own consciousness "there is nothing left", is asserted from the author's introspective catalogue. |
| [LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md) | True Believers: The Intentional Strategy and Why It Works | Dennett (1981; revised 1987, read in Mind Design II, 1997). Belief is "a perfectly objective phenomenon" that can be discerned only by one who adopts the intentional strategy. To be a true believer is to be a system "whose behavior is reliably and voluminously predictable" by it. The choice of stance is free, but its success is objective: Laplacean Martians who skipped it would miss real patterns. Thermostat and person differ only by degree. Why the strategy works is answered easily by evolution, and not yet at all by mechanism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-353](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-353.md)), in the revised text reprinted in Mind Design II (1997), not the 1981 printing; worth reading as Dennett's statement that belief is objective although only visible through a strategy: anything whose behaviour is "reliably and voluminously predictable" by the intentional strategy is a believer "in the fullest sense of the word". It turns the 1971 paper's observer-relativity ([LIT-440](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-440.md)) into "the facts about the success or failure of the stance … are perfectly objective", introduces the Martian thought experiment and the intentional "real patterns" later worked out in [LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md), and runs the thermostat-to-person continuum ("no magic moment"). Its criterion admits any system on which the strategy pays, groups included, but the essay never applies it to a group. |
| [LIT-401](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-401.md) | What is it like to be a group agent? | List (2016), DOI-10.1111/nous.12162. Group agents (firms, courts, states) are real agents in a thin functionalist sense, and they can have consciousness as awareness. Whether they have phenomenal consciousness depends on which psycho-physical bridge principle is true. Under IIT, List argues informally that a group agent's Φ is low: groups decompose into self-contained units, their steering bodies keep working when partly randomised, and most of their processing happens inside individuals. The exclusion postulate would deny group consciousness even if group Φ were high. So group agents are (close to) not conscious, which List uses to ground a normative asymmetry: groups have only derivative rights. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-340](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-340.md)); the standard reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) from the group-agency side: it grants that organised groups are agents with functional awareness and argues, conditionally on IIT, that they have little or no phenomenal consciousness. Worth reading for its separation of agency from experience and for its three reasons why a group agent's Φ should be low. The low-Φ verdict is argued informally, with no Φ computed for any group, and the paper never answers the reply Schwitzgebel had already made to the objection its third reason restates. |
| [LIT-404](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-404.md) | Does a rock implement every finite-state automaton? | Chalmers (1996), Synthese 108(3):309–333. Putnam's proof that every open system implements every finite-state automaton fails, because implementation needs reliable, counterfactual-supporting transitions for every formal state. Repaired, it survives only for weak formalisms: a clock and a dial implement every inputless FSA, and an input memory and a dial upgrade any system with the right input–output dependencies to every FSA with them. Combinatorial-state automata, whose states are vectors of independently varying components in distinct physical regions, put a strong constraint on implementation. That keeps computation available as a foundation for the theory of mind. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-342](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-342.md)), from the author's HTML copy, not the Synthese typeset text; worth reading as the standard reply to Putnam's and Searle's triviality arguments and as the source of the combinatorial-state automaton (CSA). Its result is real but partial: implementation needs counterfactual-supporting transitions over all formal states, inputless FSAs are trivially implemented by any clock plus dial, FSAs with input are implemented by any system with the right input–output dependencies plus an input memory and a dial, and CSAs escape only because a blind implementation must grow by a factor of n per step. Chalmers leaves two open problems (logically possible false implementations, and an overstrict one-region-per-component condition). For this record it decides which formalism a China-brain argument has to be stated in, and it lets one physical system host two minds. |
| [LIT-405](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-405.md) | Where Am I? | Dennett (1978), the closing essay of Brainstorms. A narrator's brain ("Yorick") is kept in a vat in Houston and radio-linked to his body ("Hamlet") under Tulsa. Where is he? Not simply where the body is, and not simply where the brain is: he cannot think "here" of the vat. He favours being wherever his point of view is, finds that unclear, and when the links fail finds himself "in Houston". A computer duplicate ("Hubert") runs in step with Yorick, and either can drive a new body with no detectable switch. The essay ends when the two drift out of step and a second person speaks through the body. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-338.md)), in a retyped course copy, not the printed book; worth reading as the founding thought experiment on where a person is when brain and body are apart, and the place the record's threads on extended vehicles, scattered individuals and functional duplicates meet. It is fiction with a philosophical argument inside it. It tries three answers to "where am I?" (where the body is, where the brain is, where the point of view is), favours the third, admits it is unclear, and ends by showing that two synchronised brains can drift into two persons. It argues by intuition pump and settles nothing; the narrator calls one of its answers a truth "of underwhelming significance". |
| [LIT-406](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-406.md) | Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (1995), Journal of Consciousness Studies 2(3):200–219. The "easy" problems of consciousness (discrimination, integration, report, access, attention, control, wakefulness) are problems of explaining functions, and a mechanism that performs a function explains it. The hard problem is that after every such function is explained, "why is the performance of these functions accompanied by experience?" stays open, so reductive methods cannot answer it. Experience should be taken as fundamental, linked to the physical by psychophysical laws. Two nonbasic candidates are offered, structural coherence (the structure of experience mirrors the structure of awareness) and organizational invariance (fine-grained functional isomorphs have the same experiences), with a speculative double-aspect theory of information as the basic law. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-336](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-336.md)); worth reading as the source of the easy/hard distinction, and short. Cite it for three separable things: the hard problem as the claim that explaining every function near experience leaves "why is this accompanied by experience?" open (§§2–3); the outline of a nonreductive theory built from two nonbasic principles, structural coherence and organizational invariance (§7); and the double-aspect theory of information, which the author calls "more of an idea than a theory" (§8). The organizational-invariance argument here is a one-page sketch; the full version is [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md). |
| [LIT-407](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-407.md) | Troubles with Functionalism | Block (1978), Minnesota Studies in the Philosophy of Science 9:261–325. Functionalism ties mental states to the world only through inputs and outputs, so it is "liberal": a body run by a billion people with radios, each implementing one line of your machine table (the nation-of-China system), would be functionally equivalent to you, yet there is prima facie doubt that it has qualia. Putnam's stipulation that no pain-feeler has parts with pain-feeler organisation is an ad hoc patch that fails on its own terms. Psychofunctionalism escapes the doubt for beliefs but perhaps not for qualia, and no specification of inputs and outputs avoids both liberalism and chauvinism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-366](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-366.md)); worth reading as the source of the homunculi-headed robot and the nation-of-China system, and of the first published objection to Putnam's anti-nesting stipulation. Cite it for two things that are easy to run together: the Absent Qualia Argument (a Functional simulation built from people is prima facie without qualia), and the case that Putnam's condition is ad hoc (§1.5). Block grounds the doubt about the China system in its being unlike us psychologically and neurally and designed to mimic us, not in its parts having minds (n. 19). He also grants that a Psychofunctional homunculi-head could have beliefs (§2.1). So it is not a source for "a whole made of minded parts cannot be conscious". |
| [LIT-409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-409.md) | How a materialist can deny that the United States is probably conscious – response to Schwitzgebel | Kammerer (2015), DOI-10.1007/s11406-015-9653-z. A short reply to [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md) proposing the Sophisticated Anti-Nesting Principle (SAP). A whole W that has a functional property P normally sufficient for a conscious state S lacks S when some part of W plays a role that (A) requires the part to have conscious states representing W and (B) is indispensable: without some part playing such a role, W would lack P. The SAP keeps Schwitzgebel's antheads and Block's tiny-people neurons conscious, admits some group consciousness, and denies it to the US, whose citizens represent the US and could not be replaced by parts that do not. It is justified by an Occam-style rule against ascribing consciousness where other subjects' states explain the behaviour. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-362](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-362.md)); the most careful anti-nesting principle in the record, and the one aimed directly at [LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md). Worth reading because it draws the line that matters for the society-of-mind bridge: a whole is denied a conscious state only when the functional organisation that would ground it runs through parts that consciously represent the whole and could not be replaced by parts that do not. Its application to the United States rests on an asserted counterfactual, and its justification is an Occam-style principle the author says needs further work. Schwitzgebel replied in Philosophia 44 (2016). |
| [LIT-413](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-413.md) | The Mind's I: Fantasies and Reflections on Self and Soul | Hofstadter & Dennett (eds.) (1981), Basic Books. An anthology of 27 selections, fiction and philosophy, on self, soul and consciousness, each followed by a "Reflections" by the editors. Among them are Turing's imitation-game paper ([LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md)), Searle's Chinese room ([LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md)), Nagel's bat ([LIT-096](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-096.md)), Dennett's "Where Am I?" and Hofstadter's "Prelude ... Ant Fugue" from GEB ([LIT-437](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-437.md)). Unread: registered from the catalogue record and a contents note; the Reflections, which are the editors' own contribution, were not seen. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the Library of Congress catalogue record, the publisher's page and a library contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scans of the 1981 Basic Books, Harvester, Bantam and Penguin printings are all lending-only, HathiTrust has no record for the LCCN, and no publisher, editor or Tufts-archive copy is posted. The editors' Reflections are unread. Two of the selections were read in full from lawful copies of their first publications and filed on their own: Turing ([LIT-394](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-394.md)) and Searle ([LIT-400](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-400.md)). |
| [LIT-415](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-415.md) | Extended Cognition and Extended Consciousness | Chalmers (2019), DOI-10.1093/oso/9780190662813.003.0002. The 1998 extended-mind thesis as stated is too weak, since opponents accept extension in wired-in "extended circuit" cases. The interesting thesis is that mental states can be partly constituted by external entities in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction with them. Consciousness does not extend this way, on the proposal that it requires information directly available for global control, and perceptually mediated availability is indirect. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-356](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-356.md)); worth reading as Chalmers's own later statement of what the extended-mind thesis of [LIT-097](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-097.md) is and where it stops. It does two things. It replaces the 1998 paper's implicit thesis, which it concedes is too weak because even the critics accept it for wired-in "extended circuit" cases, with one that requires constitution "in virtue of the subject's sensorimotor interaction" (§1). And it argues that consciousness does not extend, because consciousness needs information directly available for global control and perception makes availability indirect (§3). Both are proposals, argued in a short chapter: the thesis is offered as "extensionally correct", and the directness account is offered as an explanation of why there are no plausible cases, not as a knockdown. |
| [LIT-419](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-419.md) | Form, Function, and Feel | Lycan (1981), The Journal of Philosophy 78(1):24–50, DOI-10.2307/2025395. Filed as a statement of homuncular functionalism, the view Lycan's Wikipedia entry says he advocates, and as the reply Schwitzgebel points to against Block's nation-of-China intuition. Unread: no lawful full text was reachable, so its arguments are not stated here. | Deferred — seeded 2026-10-02 from the bibliographic records (Crossref, the Philosophy Documentation Center), not read: no lawful full text could be reached. JSTOR and PDC are paywalled, Unpaywall and Semantic Scholar list no open copy, and no author copy was found. No NOTE is filed. What it argues is known here only from how Schwitzgebel and Block's acknowledgements place it, which is not a reading. |
| [LIT-423](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-423.md) | I Am a Strange Loop | Hofstadter (2007), Basic Books. Per its publisher, an "I" is "a strange loop where the brain's symbolic and physical levels feed back into each other and flip causality upside down", and the book asks whether that "I" is real or "merely a convenient fiction", and how selves "can exist in the minds of others". Its 26 contents entries run from souls and the causal potency of patterns, through Gödel's "quintessential strange loop" and downward causality, to "How we live in each other", "Consciousness = thinking" and zombies and dualism. Unread: registered from the description and the catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-01 from the publisher's description and the Library of Congress catalogue record with its contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only, and no publisher or author copy is posted. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-425](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-425.md) | The Meta-Problem of Consciousness | Chalmers (2018), Journal of Consciousness Studies 25(9–10):6–61. The meta-problem is to explain, in terms that do not mention consciousness, why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem. It is an "easy" problem with an empirical programme. Of thirteen candidate mechanisms, the most promising is an introspective model that attributes primitive relations of awareness to primitive qualities, with a sense of acquaintance. A realist theory should explain how its basis of consciousness produces these judgments, which IIT and biological theories struggle to do. Debunking arguments for illusionism can be blocked, but a residual sense of coincidence remains. Only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, and it is false because people feel pain. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-354](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-354.md)); worth reading as the statement of the meta-problem, explaining in topic-neutral terms why we judge that consciousness poses a hard problem, and as a survey of thirteen candidate mechanisms. Cite it for four things: the meta-problem as an "easy" problem with a research programme; the meta-problem challenge to theories of consciousness, which tells against IIT and biological theories; the analysis of debunking and coincidence arguments for illusionism; and the argument that only strong illusionism dissolves the hard problem, with a Moorean rejection of strong illusionism. Its own preferred solution is offered as "closer to a fleshed-out explanandum" than an explanation. |
| [LIT-430](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-430.md) | The Intentional Stance | Dennett (1987), MIT Press. Per its publisher, the "first full-scale presentation of a theory of intentionality" Dennett had been developing for almost twenty years: we understand each other by adopting a stance, "a predictive strategy of interpretation that presupposes the rationality" of whatever we predict. Six chapters reprint papers of the 1980s, each followed by a new "Reflections" essay; the first and the last three chapters are new. Chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)). Unread: registered from the description and a catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library catalogue's contents note, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only (access-restricted, printdisabled), the MIT Press page and loc.gov were blocked, and the Tufts Digital Library holds earlier versions of several chapters as papers but not the book. Its chapter 2 is True Believers ([LIT-398](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-398.md)), read in full in its 1997 reprint, which is the revised book text. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-431](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-431.md) | Time and the Observer: The Where and When of Consciousness in the Brain | Dennett & Kinsbourne (1992), Behavioral and Brain Sciences 15(2):183–201, with open peer commentary. There is no place in the brain where "it all comes together" for consciousness. Discriminations are made once, locally, and revised in parallel "drafts", none canonical. The brain represents temporal order by content, not by the timing of its own vehicles, as a dated letter does. Colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit and Libet's timing results stop looking anomalous. Whether a revision was pre-experiential (Stalinesque) or post-experiential (Orwellian) has no answer at that scale. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-367](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-367.md)), the target article only; worth reading as the shortest complete statement of the Multiple Drafts model and of the case against "Cartesian materialism", worked out on four timing phenomena (colour phi, the cutaneous rabbit, Libet's backward referral and his delayed intention). Its sound core is the distinction between the time a content is represented and the time it represents. Its strong claim, that the Orwellian/Stalinesque distinction "need have no answer" below a few hundred milliseconds, is an argument from indistinguishability, not a demonstration. The open peer commentary (pp. 201–247) was not read. |
| [LIT-433](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-433.md) | Quining Qualia | Dennett (1988), in Marcel & Bisiach (eds.), Consciousness in Contemporary Science, OUP, pp. 42–77. Qualia as tradition has them are ineffable, intrinsic, private and directly apprehensible, and fifteen intuition pumps argue that nothing has all four. Two neurosurgical routes to an apparent colour inversion, one changing qualia and one only memory-linked reactions, feel the same from the inside. So the subject cannot know his own qualia better than an outside tester can. What is real is practical ineffability and idiosyncrasy: we refer to information-rich public properties through our own detectors of them. Hence "there simply are no qualia at all". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-357](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-357.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of qualia eliminativism and the source of the post-Cartesian side in the record's consciousness readings. It argues by fifteen intuition pumps, not by proof, and says so. Its lasting results are two: the alternative-neurosurgery and Chase-and-Sanborn cases, which show that neither the subject nor the physiologist can separate a change in qualia from a change in reactions to them; and a positive account of practical ineffability and privacy as idiosyncratic, information-rich property detection. Its conclusion, "there simply are no qualia at all", is a tactical choice of words by the author's own endnote 2, not a stronger thesis than that. |
| [LIT-434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-434.md) | Illusionism as the Obvious Default Theory of Consciousness | Dennett (2016), Journal of Consciousness Studies 23(11–12):65–72, in the issue built around Frankish's target article "Illusionism as a theory of consciousness". By its search-engine abstract, it uses a parallel with stage magic to argue that illusionism should be treated as the front runner, a conservative theory to be developed in detail. Unread: registered from bibliographic records only. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from bibliographic records, not read: no readable full text could be reached. Ingenta Connect (the publisher's host) and ResearchGate returned HTTP 403, PhilPapers and Semantic Scholar refused automated access (403 and 429), the Tufts Digital Library holds no copy, and the Wayback Machine was unreachable from here, so the archived copy of Dennett's Tufts page could not be tried. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-441](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-441.md) | The Conscious Mind: In Search of a Fundamental Theory | Chalmers (1996), Oxford University Press. Per its introduction, the book argues that consciousness cannot be reductively explained and that materialism is false, and then moves toward a nonreductive theory with fundamental psychophysical laws. Its contents run from supervenience and explanation through the irreducibility argument, naturalistic dualism and the paradox of phenomenal judgment, to coherence principles, absent, fading and dancing qualia, and information. It ends with a defence of strong AI and a no-collapse reading of quantum mechanics. Unread: registered from the author's posted contents, introduction and jacket copy. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the author's posted table of contents, introduction and jacket copy, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The author posts only those three, not draft chapters. Its two central arguments for this record are readable in their paper versions, [LIT-406](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-406.md) (the hard problem and naturalistic dualism) and [LIT-392](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-392.md) (chapter 7's organizational invariance). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-442](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-442.md) | The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity | Dennett (1992), in Kessel, Cole & Johnson (eds.), Self and Consciousness: Multiple Perspectives, Erlbaum. A self is an abstractum, "a theorist's fiction", like a centre of gravity: no part of the brain, but a well-behaved posit of interpretation. It is like a fictional character, indeterminate beyond what its "text" fixes, and a selfless process can produce one (a novel-writing robot whose story is true of it). Brains are bundles of partly autonomous systems that make themselves cohere into one autobiography; when the story coheres around two points, there are two selves. Read in a copy-edited transcription. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md)), in a third party's copy-edited transcription of the text Dennett posted, not in the Erlbaum printing; worth reading as the short, canonical statement that a self is an abstractum, a "theorist's fiction" of the same kind as a centre of gravity, posited by interpretation around which a life's narrative coheres. Read it as an analogy and two thought experiments (the novel-writing robot "Gilbert", the Updike sequel), not as an argument from evidence. Its evolutionary story of self-talk is labelled speculation, and its empirical support (Gazzaniga's split-brain work, multiple personality cases) is cited, not shown. |
| [LIT-443](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-443.md) | Consciousness Explained | Dennett (1991), Little, Brown. Per its publisher, a "full-scale exploration of human consciousness" that "refutes the traditional, commonsense theory of consciousness and presents a new model, based on a wealth of information from the fields of neuroscience, psychology, and artificial intelligence". Its fourteen contents entries run from "How are hallucinations possible?" and "A method for phenomenology", through "Multiple drafts versus the Cartesian Theater" and "The architecture of the human mind", to "Qualia disqualified" and "The reality of selves". Unread: registered from the description and the catalogue's contents note. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the catalogue record with its contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scans are lending-only (access-restricted, printdisabled), no publisher or author copy is posted, and the Tufts Digital Library holds Dennett's papers but not the book or draft chapters of it. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-445](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-445.md) | From the Phenomenology to the Mechanisms of Consciousness: Integrated Information Theory 3.0 | Oizumi, Albantakis & Tononi (2014), PLoS Computational Biology 10(5):e1003588. IIT 3.0 states five axioms of experience (existence, composition, information, integration, exclusion), turns each into a postulate about mechanisms in a state, and identifies an experience with the maximally irreducible conceptual structure of a "complex". Exclusion makes a complex a local maximum of integrated conceptual information Φ over all overlapping sets of elements, so complexes cannot overlap and no subset or superset of a complex is conscious. Worked logic-gate examples show minor complexes beside a major one, an inactive network that is conscious, a minimally conscious photodiode, and a feed-forward "zombie" functionally equivalent to a conscious system. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-365](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-365.md)), equations excepted; worth reading as the formal statement of the exclusion postulate that Schwitzgebel's 2014 manuscript ([LIT-159](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-159.md)) attacks: "of all overlapping sets of elements, only one set can be conscious", a complex being a local maximum of Φ against every overlapping set. It is IIT's anti-nesting principle, stated as a postulate and motivated only by the phenomenological exclusion axiom; the paper's Occam's-razor argument is given for exclusion within a mechanism, not between systems. It also says plainly that function does not fix consciousness, which is IIT's answer to whether agency built from parts brings experience with it. |
| [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md) | Survival and Identity | Lewis (1976), DOI-10.1525/9780520353060-002. What matters in survival is mental continuity and connectedness (the R-relation among person-stages), and it is also identity, because the two answers relate different things. Persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the I-relation (being stages of one person) is the R-relation in every possible case. Fission and fusion are two persons sharing stages, counted as one by "tensed identity"; Methuselah is a continuum of overlapping 137-year persons; degrees of personal identity come from supervaluating over cut-offs for R. Against Perry: two persons, not three, took part in a fission. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md)), from a scan of the 1976 printing posted on Andrew M. Bailey's "Papers by David Lewis" page, OCR'd here; worth reading as the four-dimensionalist reconciliation of Parfit with common sense, and the source of stage-sharing and counting by tensed identity. It agrees with Parfit that what matters is mental continuity and connectedness, the R-relation among person-stages, and denies that this conflicts with identity: persons are maximal R-interrelated aggregates of stages, so the relation of being stages of one person is the R-relation. Fission becomes two persons sharing their early stages, and degrees are handled by supervaluation. A reconciliation by redefinition of counting, which Lewis grants is "somewhat counterintuitive". |
| [LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md) | Personal Identity | Parfit (1971), DOI-10.2307/2184309. Against two beliefs, that every question about personal identity must have an answer and that important questions turn on it. In Wiggins's division case, each half-brain recipient stands in the relation that would be survival if there were only one, so "how could a double success be a failure?". What matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity is one-one and all-or-nothing. Q-memory and q-intention show the relations need not presuppose identity. Speaking of past and future selves by degree of connectedness, the principle of self-interest has no independent force. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Athens course page; worth reading as the paper that separated what matters in survival from identity, and the short original of Part III of Reasons and Persons. Its division case makes "I survive as neither" absurd and "I survive as both" incompatible with identity, so it concludes that what matters is psychological continuity and connectedness, which can branch and come in degrees, while identity cannot. It supplies q-memory, the non-branching criterion, and the vocabulary of successive selves. Its first conclusion is argued; its claim that connectedness matters more than continuity is left, in its own words, needing "more arguments than I have space to give". |
| [LIT-448](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-448.md) | The Human Animal: Personal Identity Without Psychology | Olson (1997), Oxford University Press. The book-length case for animalism. Per its abstract, "our identity over time involves no psychological facts": psychological accounts "lead to grave metaphysical problems", the arguments for them are inconclusive, and since we are animals we have "the purely biological identity conditions of animals". Its chapters run from psychology and personal identity through persistence, the case against the psychological approach, whether I was ever a fetus and whether people are animals, to the biological approach and alternatives. Unread: registered from the abstract and the contents. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's abstract, the Library of Congress record and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. Oxford Academic is subscription-only, the Internet Archive copy is lending-only, and no author copy is posted. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md) | Of Personal Identity | Hume (1739), Treatise 1.4.6, with the Appendix (1740). There is no impression of a self, "constant and invariable", so no idea of one: introspection finds only "some particular perception or other", and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". The identity we ascribe to it is "fictitious", like that of plants, ships and churches: an easy transition of the imagination along resemblance and causation, with memory discovering rather than producing it, so that hard cases are "grammatical" rather than philosophical. The Appendix retracts the account of the connecting principle: two principles he cannot reconcile or renounce leave the matter "too hard for my understanding". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md)), in the Merivale–Millican critical text on davidhume.org, with the Appendix's second thoughts (App. 10–21); worth reading as the founding statement of the bundle view and the first published retraction of it. The section finds no impression of a self, calls the mind "a bundle or collection of different perceptions", and explains our ascription of identity to it as a fiction of the imagination run on resemblance and causation, the same fiction that makes a repaired ship or a rebuilt church "the same". The Appendix then confesses that it cannot explain what unites the perceptions and leaves the problem "too hard for my understanding". The section's case is introspective and associationist; its Appendix is the clearest statement of what any bundle view owes. |
| [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) | Personal Identity | Olson (2002, rev. 2023), Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. Separates seven questions (characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology, what matters) and then takes up persistence. Three answers: psychological continuity (the majority view, repaired from Locke's memory criterion via causal dependence), brute-physical continuity (animalism), and anticriterialism. Fission forces the psychological view into multiple occupancy or a non-branching clause, which makes identity not what matters. The too-many-thinkers objection says that if we are not our animals there are two thinkers in every chair. Temporal-parts ontology may leave it indeterminate what we are. Avoids the word "self". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)); worth reading as the standard map of the analytic personal-identity debate, written by the leading animalist. It separates seven questions that are usually run together, then works the persistence question through psychological-continuity, brute-physical and anticriterialist answers, fission and the too-many-thinkers objection. It is a survey with a side: §§6–7 put the case for animalism more fully than the case against it, and the entry sets the word "self" aside, so the narrative and minimal selves are outside it. |
| [LIT-456](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-456.md) | Reply to Professor Stich | Dennett (1980), Philosophical Books 21(2):73–76, replying to Stich's critical notice of Brainstorms, "Headaches" (pp. 65–73). Accepts Stich's summary. On rationality: the norm is grounded only minimally in evolution, and full rationality is an idealisation, so personhood rests on a concept we "only imperfectly achieve". On pain: there are no pains in a mature psychology's ontology, yet people feel pain; between biting the bullet, reform and common sense (pain is like holes, voices and haircuts), the choice is "a matter of policy". Philosophy supplies the medicine for the puzzles, science the rest. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-371](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-371.md)); worth reading as Dennett's shortest statement of two positions he kept: the intentional stance grounds belief in an idealisation of rationality, so persons are believers by a standard "we already know we only imperfectly achieve"; and pain is not a good theoretical entity, yet people feel pain, a choice among biting the bullet, reform and common sense that is "in some measure a matter of policy". It is also the text behind [LIT-393](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-393.md)'s account of the homunculus essay, which it confirms: Stich's quotations stand as [LIT-393](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-393.md) gives them, and Dennett's acceptance of Stich's summary is a blanket one. |
| [LIT-458](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-458.md) | Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness | Frankish (2016), Journal of Consciousness Studies 23(11–12):11–39, the target article of the issue later published as Illusionism as a Theory of Consciousness (2017). Names "illusionism": phenomenal properties are not instantiated, and the task is the "illusion problem" of explaining why experiences seem to have them. Strong illusionism (no phenomenal properties at all, only "quasi-phenomenal" physical ones introspection misrepresents) is separated from weak illusionism (real phenomenal properties that merely seem ineffable, intrinsic, private), which it argues collapses into the strong form or into radical realism. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-384](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-384.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of illusionism under that name, and the target article that Dennett's "Illusionism as the Obvious Default Theory of Consciousness" ([LIT-434](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-434.md)) answers. It names the "illusion problem", draws the strong/weak illusionism line with "quasi-phenomenal" properties, and argues from conservatism, anomalousness and the debunking argument that strong illusionism should be the research programme. It states a programme, not a theory: by its own account it "will not propose a detailed illusionist theory" (p. 1 of the eprint), and its positive arguments are abductive and openly so. |
| [LIT-459](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-459.md) | Is the United States Phenomenally Conscious? Reply to Kammerer | Schwitzgebel (2016), DOI-10.1007/s11406-016-9725-8. Reply to Kammerer's Sophisticated Anti-Nesting Principle ([LIT-409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-409.md)), which he calls the best defence of anti-nesting he has met. Three concerns: the principle allows group consciousness and may not even exclude the US, since citizens may not consciously represent the concrete entity at issue; condition A's "required" lets a member's change of motive switch group consciousness on and off with no functional change; and the Occam-style justification either leads into causal exclusion, threatening human consciousness, or is ad hoc, and group-level explanation is often the simpler one. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-381](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-381.md)); worth reading as the direct reply to Kammerer's anti-nesting principle ([LIT-409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-409.md)), and the sharpest test so far of the line [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md) calls the best candidate on offer. Its three concerns: the principle may not exclude actual groups, because it is unclear that citizens consciously represent the entity "the United States" names; its condition A, read through "required", yields flickering group consciousness with no group-level functional change; and its Occam-style justification either generalises into the causal-exclusion problem or is ad hoc. Read from the author's manuscript of 28 April 2016, not the Springer version. |
| [LIT-461](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-461.md) | Consciousness interpreted: an interpretation of Dennett's view of consciousness | Taylor (2024), DOI-10.1080/09515089.2024.2433526. Interprets Dennett's theory of consciousness as realism about a real pattern. Consciousness is a real pattern in the brain's content-bearing states (drafts), and a user-illusion: a pattern so coarse that describing the brain through it is metaphor. On that reading multiple drafts and global workspace theory are compatible, qualia eliminativism is peripheral, the Orwellian and Stalinesque readings of masking are equally good descriptions, and first-person reports are fallible as literal descriptions of the brain but authoritative as unwitting fictions. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-379](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-379.md)); worth reading as the short, charitable reconstruction of Dennett's theory of consciousness that ties it to "Real Patterns" ([LIT-220](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-220.md)): consciousness is a real pattern in the brain's content-bearing states (drafts), of the coarse, metaphorical kind Dennett calls a user-illusion. It reconciles six claims, including multiple drafts with global workspace theory and fallibility with "dictatorial" authority. It is an interpretation offered as consistent, not as correct or as Dennett's own, and its key step on metacontrast masking is a plausibility argument. |
| [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md) | The Self and the Future | Williams (1970), DOI-10.2307/2183946. One experiment, told twice. A and B enter a machine that exchanges their memories and characters, and choose selfishly which emerging person gets $100,000 and which torture: the outcomes make "changing bodies" the natural description. Told as a series of things that will happen to me (amnesia, changed character, another's "memories", then torture), fear stays rational at every step, and the step that completes the swap changes only what happens to someone else. Undecidability and convention make the clash worse, not better. If forced to choose selfishly, pass the pain to the other body, and call it a "risk". | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md)), in a JSTOR copy of the published article posted on a University of Vermont course page; worth reading as the strongest case that first-person concern tracks the body, and the paper that made the reduplication-free body swap a problem for the psychological view. It tells one body-exchange experiment twice. Told third-personally, with choices before and reactions after, it says A and B swap bodies. Told first-personally, as a series of things that will happen to me before I am tortured, it says I am the one tortured. It argues that neither indeterminacy nor convention can resolve the clash, and ends with a "rather shaky" preference for the bodily answer, as a "risk". An argument from what fear is rational, not a theory. |
| [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md) | Of Identity and Diversity | Locke (1694), Essay II.xxvii, added in the second edition. Identity is relative to the idea the name stands for: the same mass is the same particles, the same oak or horse or man is the same continued life, and the same person is the same consciousness. A person is "a thinking intelligent being" that "can consider itself as itself", and personal identity reaches "as far as this consciousness can be extended backwards to any past action or thought". It is independent of substance, material or immaterial: the prince's consciousness in the cobbler's body is the same person but not the same man. "Person" is "a forensic term", grounding reward and punishment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md)), in the Wikisource transcription of the 1853 Troutman & Hayes reprint of the sixth-edition text, compared word by word with Project Gutenberg's; worth reading as the founding text of the psychological account of personal identity and the source of the record's whole line on what a person is. It separates the same substance, the same man and the same person, puts the person in "consciousness" extended back to past actions, and calls "person" a "forensic term". Its cases, the prince and the cobbler, the day-man and the night-man, the severed little finger, are argued from intuition, and its key relation, "the same consciousness", is never defined. |
| [LIT-466](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-466.md) | Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | Shanahan (2025), arXiv:2503.16348. Asks whether consciousness talk can be stretched to disembodied, 2024-vintage LLM agents. Their time would be discrete and discontinuous, a string of unlike beads. Their "I" has two palatable referents, the model across conversations and a self confined to one conversation that "flickers into being with each user interaction", and we may slip between them. Such selves can be edited, copied and merged, and smeared across branching simulacra. Every candidate site dissolves, which Shanahan reads as Buddhist emptiness, and turns back on human selfhood. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md)) in arXiv v3 (July 2025), the only text there is; worth reading as the one paper here that argues directly about what an LLM's self is, rather than whether it has one. Its answer: two conceptions are in play, a self sited in the model and "fleeting, flickering" selves sited in single conversations, and we may slip between them; every candidate site "dissolves upon close examination", and Shanahan takes that to the Buddhist conclusion that there is no inherent self, here or in us. It is avowedly "poetic", not literal, and its examples are invented usages, not data. |
| [LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md) | Being No One: The Self-Model Theory of Subjectivity | Metzinger (2003), MIT Press. Per its publisher, "no such things as selves exist in the world: nobody ever had or was a self. All that exists are phenomenal selves", and the phenomenal self is "the content of a 'transparent self-model'". A representationalist and functional analysis of the conscious first-person perspective, with conceptual "tools", constraints on consciousness and neurophenomenological case studies (agnosia, neglect, blindsight, hallucination), asking whether being someone can be analysed at subpersonal levels. Unread: registered from the description and the contents; the theory is read in [LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md). | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text of the book could be reached. The MIT Press Direct edition is not open access and no author copy is posted. Its theory is read in Metzinger's own short statement, "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md), read in full), and more fully in his "Précis: Being No One" (PSYCHE 11(5), 2005; LIT-568, read in full 2026-10-03), the read substitute for the book, which sets out six of its ten constraints and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-468](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-468.md) | The Constitution of Selves | Schechtman (1996), Cornell University Press. Separates the reidentification question (is this the same person?) from the characterization question (which actions, experiences and traits are this person's own?), and argues against analytic philosophy's attention to the first at the expense of the second. Chapters 1–3 take up reidentification; chapters 4–6 give the narrative self-constitution view, on which, as Strawson quotes it, a person "creates his identity [only] by forming an autobiographical narrative". The source of the term "characterization question" in the SEP map. Unread: registered from the description and the contents. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, the Library of Congress record and the chapter list on Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Cornell/De Gruyter eBook is sold, not open, and the Internet Archive copy is for print-disabled users only. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-469](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-469.md) | Reasons and Persons | Parfit (1984), Clarendon Press; DOI-10.1093/019824908X.001.0001 is the 1986 reprint online. Four loosely connected parts, per the author's abstract: self-defeating theories of rationality and morality; what one person can rationally want at different times, and attitudes to time; personal identity, where "most of us … have certain beliefs about this subject that are false, but hard to give up"; and obligations to future generations, with the non-identity problem and the Repugnant Conclusion. By the chapter abstracts, Part III defends a reductionist view on which identity is not what matters and draws consequences for self-interest and distributive justice. Unread. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description, its chapter abstracts and the table of contents; the book is in copyright and no lawful full text was reachable (the Internet Archive copies are lending-only and were not opened), so it is unread and no NOTE is filed. By its publisher's account, Part III argues that most of us hold false beliefs about personal identity, that psychological continuity and connectedness, not identity, is what matters, and that this should change our attitudes to our own future, to rationality and to morality. The record already leans on it at second hand: Birch's Relation R, Velleman's reading of Frankfurt and the identity-and-ethics survey all cite it. |
| [LIT-470](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-470.md) | Foundations for a Social Ontology | Thomasson (2003), ProtoSociology 18–19:269–290. Per its abstract: the social world poses a metaphysical puzzle (how facts and objects created by human intentionality can be real) and an epistemological one (how such products can include objective facts for the social sciences to discover). Searle's account in The Construction of Social Reality is too narrow to solve either; rules for constructing social reality that parallel rules for make-believe give a more comprehensive ontology, but talk of social reality is not pretence. Unread: filed from the abstract. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's abstract; no lawful full text was reachable (the Philosophy Documentation Center sells it at $20, PhilPapers returned 403, and the Academia.edu copy sits behind a bot check), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. By its abstract it argues that Searle's account of social facts is too narrow and that rules modelled on the rules of make-believe give a fuller social ontology; how, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-475](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-475.md) | The Social Construction of What? | Hacking (1999), Harvard University Press. A book on social-construction claims whose title asks what they are claims about. By its chapter titles: why ask what; too many metaphors; the natural sciences; madness; kind-making; weapons research; rocks; the end of Captain Cook. Unread: filed from bibliographic records and the table of contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the Crossref records for the book and its chapters and the Open Library records of its editions; no lawful full text was reachable (Harvard University Press and JSTOR pages did not load, the e-book is licensed through JSTOR, and there is no author-posted draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. Its title asks of social-construction claims what they are claims about; what its answer is, beyond its chapter titles, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) | The Ant Trap: Rebuilding the Foundations of the Social Sciences | Epstein (2015), DOI-10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199381104.001.0001. Social science works with an "anthropocentric" picture on which the social world is built out of people, as an ant colony is built out of ants. Part One separates the facts that ground a social fact from the facts that anchor the frame principle saying how such facts are grounded, and argues ontological individualism false. Part Two argues that even facts about groups, including group action and intention, are grounded in more than the members. Unread: filed from the introduction, the author's précis and the publisher's description. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the author's own posted introduction and table of contents, not read: the book is not lawfully readable in full online (Oxford Academic is paywalled; the author posts only the introduction). The introduction and the author's open-access précis were read. Its framework, grounding versus anchoring, is stated in the record from the précis and from the author's SEP entry ([LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md), read). Part Two argues that facts about groups, including their actions and intentions, are grounded in more than their members, which bears directly on [THEORY-043](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-043.md). It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied. |
| [LIT-479](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-479.md) | What are groups? | Ritchie (2012 online; Philosophical Studies 166(2), 2013). Six criteria any theory of groups must meet: members can differ across times and worlds, groups exist contingently and temporarily, are located, and coincident groups of one kind can be distinct. Groups as non-singular pluralities, fusions, aggregates (Burge) and sets (Effingham) each fail at least one. Proposed instead: a group is a realization of a structure of functionally defined nodes, existing while every node is occupied; identity at a time needs the same members and the same relations. A sketch; it is silent on agency and minds. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-390](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-390.md)); worth reading as the cleanest statement of what a metaphysics of organised groups has to deliver and why pluralities, fusions, aggregates and sets fail to. Its six criteria (members can change across times and worlds, groups are contingent and located, and coincident groups of one kind can be distinct) are the useful part, and the case against each rival is short and checkable. Its own view, groups as realizations of structures whose nodes are functionally defined, is sketched in four pages; it says nothing about agency or minds, and the author amended its membership definition in her 2018 paper ([LIT-486](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-486.md)). |
| [LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md) | Gender and Race: (What) Are They? (What) Do We Want Them To Be? | Haslanger (2000), Noûs 34(1):31–55. Distinguishes conceptual, descriptive and analytical answers to "what is gender/race?" and takes the analytical one: define the terms for what a feminist antiracist theory needs. S is a woman iff S is regularly observed or imagined to have bodily features presumed to indicate a female's reproductive role, this marks S in the dominant ideology for subordinate positions, and that plays a role in S's subordination; men and racialized groups are defined in parallel, ethnicity and gender in general as the non-hierarchical genus. Stipulative by design; no evidence offered. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-394](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-394.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of ameliorative ("analytical") social ontology and of gender and race as hierarchical social positions. It is short and explicit about its method: it defines woman, man and racialized group for the purposes of a feminist and antiracist theory, says so, and accepts the consequences (non-oppressed females are not women in its sense, and the goal is a world with none). Read it for the three-way distinction between conceptual, descriptive and analytical projects and for the definitional schema (marked by assumed bodily features, positioned by a dominant ideology, subordinated or privileged as a result), not for evidence: its "matters of established fact" about race are asserted without citation, and its definitions are stipulated, not discovered. |
| [LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md) | Social ontology: Some basic principles | Searle (2006), DOI-10.1177/1463499606061731. Institutional reality is built from three primitives: collective intentionality, the assignment of function, and constitutive rules of the form "X counts as Y in C". The Y status is held only by collective acceptance, and it carries deontic powers, which are desire-independent reasons for action. Institutional facts need language because they exist only as represented. Two revisions of the 1995 book: status indicators (after De Soto), and "free-standing Y terms" (after Barry Smith), such as corporations and money without currency. In those cases there is no X, and "We accept (S has power (S does A))", a formula from later in the book, is ranked as the more general form. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-388](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-388.md)), in its parallel English printing in Papers: Revista de Sociologia 80 (2006), pp. 51–71, not in the Anthropological Theory typesetting the DOI names; worth reading as Searle's own short restatement of The Construction of Social Reality ([LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md)), and as the place where he concedes that "X counts as Y in C" is not the general form. Status functions imposed by collective acceptance carry deontic powers, and deontic powers are desire-independent reasons for action. Read it for the structure, not for an argument about collective intentionality: that is taken as a primitive and referred to his 1990 paper ([LIT-490](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-490.md)), not defended here. |
| [LIT-484](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-484.md) | Qu'est-ce qu'un fait social ? | Durkheim (1894; book 1895), ch. I of Les Règles de la méthode sociologique. A social fact is "toute manière de faire, fixée ou non, susceptible d'exercer sur l'individu une contrainte extérieure", or equivalently one general in a society while existing independently of its individual manifestations. Such facts are neither organic nor individual-psychic, so their substrate is society. They are general because collective, not collective because general: "il est dans chaque partie parce qu'il est dans le tout". Ways of being (morphology) are consolidated ways of doing. A definition argued from examples, not proved. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-391](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-391.md)); worth reading as the founding definition of a social fact, and as a short text later social ontology still cites (Ritchie 2018 does, for the group as more than a sum). Fifteen pages define the object of sociology by two marks, exteriority to individual consciousness and external constraint, with diffusion plus independent existence as an equivalent second test. It is a definition, not an argument: Durkheim calls it "un simple résumé des données immédiates de lobservation" (n. 3), and its two load-bearing steps (that what is neither organic nor individual-psychic must have society as its substrate, and that constraint is present even where nobody feels it) are asserted from examples. Read for the vocabulary and the part-whole thesis ("il est dans chaque partie parce qu'il est dans le tout"), not for a proof. |
| [LIT-485](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-485.md) | The Construction of Social Reality | Searle (1995), Free Press, New York (xiii + 241 pp.). The founding book of Searle's social ontology. Per its catalogue description, it argues that some facts are independent of human observers and some require human agreement. Its chapters move from the building blocks of social reality and the creation of institutional facts through language and a general theory of institutional facts, to a defence of external realism and the correspondence theory of truth. Unread: filed from the catalogue record and contents; the record reads the theory in Searle's 2006 restatement. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from catalogue records and a library scan of the table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in print with Free Press / Simon & Schuster, the Internet Archive copies are either lending-only or unauthorised uploads, and Searle posted no draft), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. The record reads the theory through Searle's own 2006 restatement ([LIT-482](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-482.md), read in full), which is the entry to start from. |
| [LIT-486](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-486.md) | Social Structures and the Ontology of Social Groups | Ritchie (2018 online; PPR 100(2), 2020). Social structures are networks of relations constitutively, not merely causally, dependent on social factors, and can be overt or covert, intentionally or unintentionally created, internal or external to what realizes them. Organized social groups (teams, courts, families) are structured wholes with internal social structures whose nodes people occupy; feature social groups (women, racial groups, classes) are social kinds, nodes in external social structures. Both meet a "Goldilocks Constraint": intuitive and explanatory groups in, arbitrary collections out. Silent on agency. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-389](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-389.md)); worth reading as the one framework in the record that covers both kinds of social group, the organised ones the group-agency literature is about and the race, gender and class groups the social-construction literature is about, and says why they differ. Organized social groups (teams, courts, firms) are structured wholes with internal social structures; feature social groups (women, African Americans, economic classes) are social kinds, nodes in external social structures. It is a framework offered to "motivate", not a proof, and its anti-overgeneration work is done by a restriction to structures that "intuitively exist" or "figure in explanations", imported rather than derived. It says nothing about agency or minds. |
| [LIT-487](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-487.md) | Social Ontology | Epstein (2018; rev. 2024), <https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/social-ontology/>. A survey that splits social ontology into two inquiries: what determines (grounds) a social fact, and what constructs or "anchors" the category it falls under, likened to semantics and metasemantics. §3 surveys determination bases (psychologism, atomism, bodies and practices, physicalism, holism, flat ontologies) and reports that ontological individualism is widely assumed and recently contested. §4 surveys anchoring theories (agreement, Lewis's convention, Hart and Searle's collective acceptance, patterns, practices, language). §5 covers groups, group minds and agency, institutions, race and gender, artifacts, money, law and language. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-393](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-393.md)); worth reading as a survey: the best single map of social ontology in the record, organised around its author's distinction between what grounds a social fact (§3) and what anchors, or sets up, the category it falls under (§4). It is also the record's readable source for what The Ant Trap's grounding–anchoring framework is ([LIT-478](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-478.md) is not lawfully readable). Read it as a survey written by a partisan: Epstein's own positions organise the entry, and the critics of anchoring are named but given a sentence each. |
| [LIT-491](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-491.md) | Categories We Live By: The Construction of Sex, Gender, Race, and Other Social Categories | Ásta (2018), OUP. Per its publisher, a theory of social categories built on the question "what is it for a feature of an individual to be socially meaningful?"; its main idea is that "social categories are conferred upon people", and its "conferralist" framework is applied to sex, gender, race, disability and other categories, and to their tendency to oppress. Unread: filed from the description and contents only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and table of contents; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is not open access, Oxford Academic is paywalled, and the author's site posts replies and related essays but no chapters or drafts), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the book-length statement of conferralism, the main rival to Haslanger's account of social categories ([LIT-480](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-480.md)); what it argues beyond the description is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md) | Time, Structure and Fluctuations | Prigogine (1977), Nobel Lecture, reprinted in Science 201:777 (1978). Near equilibrium the second-order excess entropy δ²S is a Lyapounov function, so fluctuations die out, and in the "strictly" linear regime the steady state minimizes entropy production. Far from equilibrium the sign of the excess entropy production ΣδJδX is no longer fixed. Given autocatalytic steps (necessary, not sufficient) the thermodynamic branch can go unstable, and fluctuations are amplified into "dissipative structures": Bénard convection, the Brusselator's limit cycle and "Turing bifurcation". A closing programme derives irreversibility from a non-unitary transformation of the Liouville dynamics. | Active — read in full 2026-10-02 ([NOTE-424](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-424.md)); worth reading as Prigogine's own short statement of the dissipative-structure programme, and as the place where its scope limits are stated in his words. A dissipative structure is a state beyond an instability of the "thermodynamic branch", "a giant fluctuation stabilized by exchanges of energy with the outside world". The minimum-entropy-production theorem is valid only in the "strictly" linear regime with constant phenomenological coefficients. Far from equilibrium the only general criterion offered is a sufficient one for stability (non-negative excess entropy production). Its §§6–7 programme of a non-unitary "entropy operator" is a sketch whose demonstrated link to macroscopic thermodynamics is, by its own account, "at least in the linear region". |
| [LIT-529](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-529.md) | Incomplete Nature: How Mind Emerged from Matter | Deacon (2011), W. W. Norton. An account of how life, mind and purpose ("ententional" phenomena) emerged from physics, built on constraint and absence rather than on added stuff. Its contents run from absence, homunculi and teleonomy through emergence and constraint to a hierarchy of dynamics (homeodynamics, morphodynamics, teleodynamics), a minimal self-producing system (autogenesis), and then work, information, significance, evolution, self, sentience and consciousness. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the contents; the text was not reached. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and a library contents note, not read: no lawful full text could be reached. The Internet Archive scan of the Norton printing is lending-only, and no author-posted draft was found. The companion chapter the record already cites, Deacon & Cashman (2013), "Teleology versus mechanism in biology: beyond self-organization", is identified below but was not reachable either and is not filed. |
| [LIT-534](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-534.md) | Order Out of Chaos: Man's New Dialogue with Nature | Prigogine & Stengers (1984), Bantam; based on their La nouvelle alliance. A book for general readers that sets the science of complexity and irreversibility against classical dynamics. By its contents: the rise and limits of Newtonian science and its philosophical reception (Diderot, Kant, Hegel, Bergson, Whitehead); thermodynamics from Carnot to Boltzmann's order principle; linear and far-from-equilibrium thermodynamics, bifurcations and order through fluctuations; and the rediscovery of time in physics. Unread: filed from catalogue records only. | Deferred — filed 2026-10-02 from library catalogue records and a partial contents note; no lawful full text was reachable (the book is in copyright, the Internet Archive scans of the Bantam and Flamingo printings are lending-only, HathiTrust is search-only), so it is not read and no NOTE is filed. It is the popular and philosophical statement of the programme whose technical core is the Nobel lecture ([LIT-516](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-516.md)); what it argues, beyond its contents, is not recorded here. |
| [LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md) | Biological Autonomy: A Philosophical and Theoretical Enquiry | Moreno & Mossio (2015), Springer, History, Philosophy and Theory of the Life Sciences 12. The book argues that biology should revolve around autonomy, not only natural selection: organisms are organized systems that self-produce and self-maintain as integrated wholes, set their own goals and norms, and promote the conditions of their existence through interaction with their environment. Chapters treat constraints and organisational closure, emergence and inter-level causation, teleology and function, agency, evolution, organisms and levels of autonomy, and cognition. Unread: registered from the publisher's description and the chapter list. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-02 from the publisher's description and the chapter list, not read. The book is not open access at Springer, but the authors deposited a copy of it in HAL (hal-01151449, "Book_Autonomy_web.pdf", CC BY-NC 4.0, deposited 13 May 2015). HAL now serves files behind an anti-bot challenge that requires a browser running JavaScript, and it states that the challenge is there against automated scrapers, so I did not try to get past it. A human reader can open the copy lawfully, and a reading from it would move this to Active. |
| [LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md) | Explanatory Models for Psychiatric Illness | Kendler (2008), American Journal of Psychiatry 165(6):695–702. Psychiatry should explain by mechanisms, not laws. Psychiatric causes act at many levels, within and outside the person, and are non-aggregative and loop-ridden, as an alcohol-dependence sketch shows (gene–environment interaction, tolerance feedback, niche selection, aversive cultural transmission). So "hard reductionism" and "hard emergentism" both fail, but locally decomposable subsystems can still be studied and then reassembled.
