After Marr, biology will implement psychological functions, not replace them. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-432](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-432.md)), from the NIH author manuscript in PubMed Central; filed as the readable substitute for Kendler's 2005 "Toward a Philosophical Structure for Psychiatry" ([LIT-552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-552.md)), which has no lawful open copy. It opens by citing the 2005 paper for its premise that etiological models must be pluralistic, and develops two of the 2005 abstract's propositions at length: piecemeal integration becomes "decomposition and reassembly" of multilevel mechanisms, and the mind–brain question becomes Marr-style implementation, in which "biology will implement but not replace psychology". It does not restate the 2005 paper's arguments against dualism and epiphenomenalism, so it stands in for the pluralism, not for the whole of the earlier paper. |
| [LIT-552](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-552.md) | Toward a Philosophical Structure for Psychiatry | Kendler (2005), American Journal of Psychiatry 162(3):433–440. Eight propositions for a philosophical frame for psychiatry, per the abstract: psychiatry is grounded in first-person experience; Cartesian substance dualism and epiphenomenalism are false; brain→mind and mind→brain causation are both real; psychiatric disorders are etiologically complex, with no more "spirochete-like" discoveries to come; explanatory pluralism beats monism, especially biological reductionism; and the goal is "patchy reductionism" and "piecemeal integration". Unread: registered from its PubMed abstract. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from its PubMed abstract and Crossref, not read. Not open access: Unpaywall lists no open copy, Europe PMC and PubMed Central hold no full text, and psychiatryonline.org answered both the full-text page and the PDF with HTTP 403 and a Cloudflare "Just a moment" challenge, which I did not try to get past. A web search finds it only on a document-sharing site, which is not an author or institutional deposit. A reader with American Journal of Psychiatry access can read it lawfully; a reading would move this to Active. Its readable substitute is Kendler's "Explanatory models for psychiatric illness" (Am J Psychiatry 165(6):695–702, 2008), filed and read in full as [LIT-539](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-539.md). That paper cites this one for its pluralist premise and develops its piecemeal integration and its mind–brain propositions, but not its arguments against dualism and epiphenomenalism. A later open paper, "The dappled nature of causes of psychiatric illness" (Mol Psychiatry 17(4):377–388, 2012, PMC3312951), was not read or filed. |
| [LIT-560](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-560.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | Ryan & Deci (2006), Journal of Personality 74(6):1557–1586. SDT's defence of autonomy as a psychological construct. Philosophers (phenomenologists from Pfänder and Ricoeur; hierarchical accounts from Frankfurt and Dworkin) agree that autonomy is self-endorsement, not independence. On that definition, the critiques fail: behaviourists and Bandura define autonomy as independence from the environment; reductive neuroscience mistakes levels of explanation; nonconscious priming shows autonomy can be compromised, not that it is illusory; too many options is not self-determination; and autonomy matters across cultures. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md)), from the authors' own deposit of the published article on selfdeterminationtheory.org; worth reading as the place where SDT states its concept of autonomy against both philosophy and psychology. Autonomy is "regulation by the self", its opposite "heteronomy", regulation "without self-endorsement" (abstract). It is "a matter of degree" (p. 1562), compatible with dependence and with having one option, and lies "not in being independent causes but in exercising their capacity to reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). It answers Skinner, Bandura, Pinker, Bargh, Wegner, Schwartz and Iyengar. Its engagement with Frankfurt is thin: two citations of the 1971 paper inside one paragraph on hierarchical accounts, with the analytic detail taken from Dworkin. |
| [LIT-568](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-568.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger (2005), PSYCHE 11(5), the author's précis of Being No One. Minimal consciousness is a global world-model in a window of presence that cannot be recognised as a model (globality, presentationality, transparency). A phenomenal self is a transparent self-model: "no such things as selves exist in the world". Transparency comes in degrees, and the self-model's opaque partition is what lets humans doubt their own self-representation. The unity of consciousness is a single global functional cluster. A first-person perspective is a phenomenal model of the intentionality relation, and iterating it yields introspective and social intelligence. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md)), as the read substitute for Being No One ([LIT-467](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-467.md)), which it summarises in Metzinger's own words. Worth reading as the most complete short statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity (SMT): more of the machinery than "Self models" ([LIT-450](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-450.md)), in particular the six constraints, the degrees of transparency, and the phenomenal model of the intentionality relation (PMIR). Phenomenal selfhood is a transparent self-model, "a function realized by a lack of information"; "no such things as selves exist in the world". The unity of a conscious world is a global functional cluster bound by "highest-order binding". It states the theory and its predictions; the evidence is cited, not shown, and the neural sections say how little is known. |
| [LIT-582](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-582.md) | Biological organisation as closure of constraints | Montévil & Mossio (2015), J. Theor. Biol. 372:179–191. Two causal regimes act in organisms: processes (thermodynamic changes) and constraints, which act on processes while being conserved at the relevant time scale. Closure is mutual dependence among constraints: each is produced by a process another constraint constrains, and each helps produce another. Closure mixes slow and fast dependence, grounds functions, and is proposed as a boundary criterion. A volume-sweeping count of dependencies, the tendency to closure, separates symbionts that share an encompassing closure, and separated nested closures mark levels of organisation. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-468](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-468.md)), from the authors' HAL deposit of the accepted text. Worth reading as the paper statement of the central claim of Biological Autonomy ([LIT-536](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-536.md)): biological organisation is closure of constraints. A constraint is defined by a symmetry: it acts on a process at a time scale at which it is itself conserved. Closure is a set of constraints each of which depends directly on another in the set and generates another, and cannot be split into two closed sets. The paper offers closure as a boundary criterion and gives a preliminary measure, the tendency to closure, for drawing boundaries between interacting organisms. It does not claim closure defines an organism. |
| [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md) | The Normative Constitution of Agency | Korsgaard (2014), in Rational and Social Agency: The Philosophy of Michael Bratman (OUP), pp. 190–214. Two conceptions of agency are set side by side: natural (action is movement caused by the right mental state) and normatively constituted (action is movement backed by a unified agent, whose unity is achieved by following norms). Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action "the form of self-determined efficacy". Choosing maxims under that form constitutes one's practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes sets the task of unification. Unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", so people can literally act together. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-455](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-455.md)), in the author's posted manuscript, not the typeset chapter. Worth reading as the read substitute for Self-Constitution (2009, [LIT-597](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-597.md)), which it summarises and extends, and as Korsgaard's direct engagement with Bratman. Agency is "normatively constituted": an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and that unity is achieved by following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives, which give action "the form of self-determined efficacy". The content of the maxims we choose under that form constitutes our "practical identities". So "we make ourselves into agents", and unity of agency, individual or collective, "is an achievement, not a given". Argued, not proved; the account of reason as unification is said to be "lifted" from her other work. |
| [LIT-603](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-603.md) | The Emperor's New Markov Blankets | Bruineberg, Dołęga, Dewhurst & Baltieri (2020 preprint; BBS 45:e183, 2022). Markov blankets entered variational inference as Pearl's conditional-independence shields, tools on a scientist's map. In the free-energy literature since Friston 2013 they became boundaries in the world between agent and environment: "Friston blankets". The two are different constructs; Friston blankets need extra assumptions (a chosen internal node, sensorimotor labels, steady state, sparse coupling) that the formalism does not supply. Using them for metaphysical conclusions ("inference within a model") requires metaphysical premises; used instrumentally ("inference with a model") they are innocent but philosophically idle. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-447](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-447.md)), but in its December 2020 PhilSci-Archive version; the Behavioral and Brain Sciences target article of 2021–2022 is, by the authors' own note, "heavily rewritten" and could not be read lawfully beyond its abstract. Worth reading as the critique that names the problem: "Pearl blankets", the conditional-independence tool of graphical models, are conflated with "Friston blankets", a realist construct meant to be the boundary between an agent and its world. The second cannot be read off the mathematics of the first, and its use to settle questions about life and mind needs metaphysical premises of its own. It re-runs the primordial-soup simulation of [LIT-526](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-526.md) and shows how the blanket found there depends on modelling choices. |
| [LIT-630](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-630.md) | The Mind as the Software of the Brain | Block (1995), in Smith & Osherson (eds.), An Invitation to Cognitive Science, 2nd ed., vol. 3, Thinking, MIT Press, ch. 11, pp. 377–425. The computer model explains intelligence by decomposing it into ever stupider processors that bottom out in primitive processors, the only devices for which behaviourism is true. The brain is a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, by an isomorphism between symbol transitions and rational relations among meanings, which must hold counterfactually, so a wall is not every computer. Intentionality comes from the language of thought plus functional role semantics. Stich's syntactic theory falls to the "Reductionist Cruncher", and the systems reply answers Searle, though Block doubts the Chinese system is phenomenally conscious. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-490](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-490.md)); worth reading as Block's textbook statement of what "the mind is the software of the brain" means: intelligence explained by functional decomposition into primitive processors, the brain as a syntactic engine driving a semantic engine, intentionality explained by the language of thought plus functional role semantics, and the defence of that picture against Dennett's objections, Stich's syntactic theory (by the "Reductionist Cruncher") and Searle's Chinese room. It is a survey for an introductory volume, so its arguments are compressed, but it states clearly two things the record uses: intelligence is future-oriented and intentionality past-oriented, and the computer model may give intentionality without phenomenal consciousness. |
| [LIT-632](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-632.md) | Comparing the Major Theories of Consciousness | Block (2009), in Gazzaniga (ed.), The Cognitive Neurosciences, 4th ed., MIT Press, ch. 77, pp. 1111–1122. Compares the three theories neuroscientists take most seriously: higher-order thought, the global workspace and the biological theory. Only the biological theory fully acknowledges the explanatory gap; the others replace it with a puzzle their own theory creates. Concept dualism stops the gap becoming dualism. The ambitious higher-order theory also fails on stipulation, mismatch and infants. Integrated information is criticised as a theory of intelligence. The biological theory is the least friendly to machine consciousness. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-505](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-505.md)); worth reading as Block's comparison of the higher-order thought, global workspace and biological theories by one test: does the theory recognise the explanatory gap? The ambitious higher-order theory and the workspace theory turn the gap into a puzzle of their own making, so only the biological theory "fully acknowledges" it; concept dualism keeps that from becoming dualism. Also the source of the "biological theory" that Chalmers's meta-problem paper cites as "Block 2009", and a short argument that the biological theory is less friendly to machine consciousness than its rivals. |
| [LIT-634](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-634.md) | Inverted Earth | Block (1990), Philosophical Perspectives 4:53–79. Inverted Earth has complementary colours and inverted colour words, so a visitor with colour-inverting lenses notices nothing. After long residence, or for a twin raised there with a molecule-for-molecule identical brain, the intentional content of the experience of the sky inverts (it is about yellow) and so does its functional role in a long-arm description, while qualitative content stays the same. So qualitative content is not a functional state and the intentional/qualitative distinction stands. Public colour terms like "looks red" express intentional, not qualitative, content. A brain-internal functional theory of qualia would escape, but nobody has said what it is. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-504](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-504.md)); worth reading as the source of the Inverted Earth argument: a subject moved, unaware, to a planet of complementary colours and inverted colour words keeps the same qualitative content while, over time, the intentional content and the (long-arm) functional role of the experience invert. That is the converse of the inverted spectrum, and it needs no internal switch, so the subject's testimony is undisturbed and brain supervenience is on the qualia realist's side. It refutes functionalism about qualia only in its long-arm form; Block concedes a short-arm functional theory of qualia would sink it, and answers that only with a burden of proof. |
| [LIT-635](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-635.md) | Mental Paint | Block (2003), in Hahn & Ramberg (eds.), Reflections and Replies, MIT Press, pp. 165–200. Phenomenal character outruns representational content. Internalist representationism must find a functional difference for every phenomenal one, and Erisa, raised where colours keep changing, has vivid colour differences with no abiding functional ones. Against externalist representationism: a swampman has phenomenal character and no content; attention is not awareness, so transparency fails as a claim about awareness; on Inverted Earth what stays the same is mental paint; and normal variation in colour vision means, if representationism is true, that a standard chip cannot look its shade to both men and women. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-511](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-511.md)); worth reading as Block's fullest case against representationism about phenomenal character ("phenomenism" against "representationism"). It separates mental paint (phenomenal properties that represent) from mental oil (phenomenal properties that do not), argues against internalist representationism with Erisa, raised among colours that keep changing, and against externalist representationism with Inverted Earth, long-term memory, and an empirical "shifted spectra" argument from normal variation in cone sensitivity and in where people place unique green. Several of its arguments are offered as pressure, not proof, and Block says so. |
| [LIT-639](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-639.md) | The Harder Problem of Consciousness | Block (2002), The Journal of Philosophy 99(8):391–425. For anyone who is both a naturalist (physicalism is the default) and a phenomenal realist (consciousness is real and not defined by function), a merely superficial functional isomorph of us with a different physical basis, "Commander Data", poses a harder problem than the hard one. We have no conception of evidence that could show whether he is conscious, so physicalism is the default yet inaccessible, and it is the subjective default that he is not conscious though the question is open. Disjunctive or functional bases would save naturalism but could never be known. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-501](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-501.md)); worth reading as the argument that whether a functional duplicate of us made of different stuff is conscious is not just unknown but "meta-inaccessible": we have no conception of evidence that would settle it. For a naturalist who is also a phenomenal realist, physicalism is the default and yet whether such a being is conscious cannot bear on it. The paper also dissolves one form of the hard problem by treating subjective and objective as properties of concepts, not of properties. It lays out the tension and argues for no way out. |
| [LIT-641](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-641.md) | What Psychological States are Not | Block & Fodor (1972), The Philosophical Review 81(2):159–181. Behaviourism and type physicalism set type-identity conditions on psychological states that are too concrete, and the decisive arguments against them are empirical. The functional state identity theory (FSIT), on which each psychological state is a machine-table state of the organism's unique best description as a probabilistic automaton, fails too. It cannot model dispositions that are never occurrent, simultaneous states, or a productive and structured set of states, and it individuates too finely. Inverted or absent qualia are a prima facie objection to any functional definition. Psychological states look like computational states, not machine-table states, and type identity is fixed by the laws the states fall under. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-491](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-491.md)); worth reading as the first sustained case against machine-state functionalism, and as the place where the inverted- and absent-qualia objection is first set down as an objection to functional definitions of mental states. Its central result is narrower than "functionalism is false": psychological states cannot be put one-to-one with the machine-table states of a probabilistic automaton (§III, arguments 1, 2, 4, 5, 6), though they may correspond to computational states. Only the qualia argument (3) threatens functionalism in the broad sense, and the authors treat it as prima facie. |
| [LIT-642](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-642.md) | Psychologism and Behaviorism | Block (1981), The Philosophical Review 90(1):5–43. Psychologism, the doctrine that whether behaviour is intelligent depends on the information processing that produces it, is true. A machine that stores all sensible conversations of a test's length and looks up its replies has the capacity to respond sensibly to any sequence of inputs, so it satisfies the strongest behaviourist conception of intelligence, yet all its intelligence is its programmers'. The standard objections to behaviourism (Chisholm–Geach, the perfect actor, paralytics) defeat behaviourist necessary conditions but not sufficient ones; this machine defeats the sufficient condition. Psychologism is not chauvinism: it excludes one kind of processing without requiring ours. | Active — read in full 2026-10-03 ([NOTE-506](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-506.md)); worth reading as the source of the "Blockhead": a machine that stores every sensible hour-long conversation and so has the capacity to pass any Turing test of that length, yet "has the intelligence of a toaster". The argument refutes behaviourist sufficient conditions for intelligence, including a capacity version that survives the standard objections, and establishes psychologism: whether behaviour is intelligent depends partly on the processing that produces it. It does not say which processing is required, only that it needs some "richness", and the closing case against simulators of physics, neurons or psychology is admitted to be a sketch. |
| [LIT-685](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-685.md) v2 | Freedom Within Reason | Wolf (1990), Oxford University Press. Unread seed. The book-length Reason View: free will is "the freedom to be good, or the freedom to do the right thing for the right reasons" (publisher's abstract). It sets up the dilemma of autonomy, argues that the Real Self View (Hume, Frankfurt, Watson, Taylor) and the Autonomy View both fail, states the Reason View, defends its notion of ability against determinism, and asks what the True and the Good must be for the view to hold. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 as a seed, from Crossref's book and chapter records (whose abstracts are each chapter's opening paragraph), the SEP entry the record holds and an MIT lecture handout, not read. No lawful full text was found: the book is paywalled at Oxford Academic, Unpaywall lists no open copy (oa_status closed), and no author or repository deposit turned up. A person with Oxford Academic or library access can supply it (Oxford University Press, 1990, 153 pp., DOI 10.1093/oso/9780195056167.001.0001); chapter 4, "The Reason View" (pp. 67–93), and chapter 2, "The Real Self View" (pp. 23–45), are the parts to read first. |
| [LIT-688](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-688.md) v2 | Asymmetrical Freedom | Wolf (1980), The Journal of Philosophy 77(3):151–166. Unread. By the SEP's report it is the origin of the Reason View's asymmetry: an agent who acts in accord with the True and the Good is praiseworthy even if psychologically determined so that she could not have done otherwise, but one who acts against it is blameworthy only if she could have done otherwise. Blame therefore needs regulative control and praise needs only guidance control, and Wolf answers the threat from determinism by denying that physical determination entails psychological determination. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-03 from Crossref, the record's own second-hand readings and the SEP entry it already holds, not read. | [LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md) | Freedom of the Will and the Concept of a Person | Frankfurt (1971), The Journal of Philosophy 68(1):5–20. What is essential to a person is the structure of the will. A person's will is the effective first-order desire, the one that moves him "all the way to action" (p. 8). A second-order volition is wanting a desire to be one's will; persons have them, and wantons, who "do not care" about their wills, do not (pp. 10–11). Forming one is identifying with one desire and withdrawing from another (p. 13). Freedom of the will is having the will one wants, "securing the conformity of his will to his second-order volitions" (p. 15), and a decisive identification "resounds" through all higher orders (p. 16). Moral responsibility needs neither a free will nor alternatives: the willing addict acts "of his own free will" (pp. 18–20). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-545.md)); worth reading as the source of the hierarchical account of the will, which the record has so far held only second-hand: first- and second-order desires, the will as the effective desire, second-order volitions, wantons and persons, freedom of the will as having the will one wants, decisive identification that "resounds" through higher orders, and a responsibility that needs neither a free will nor alternatives. Read it knowing that it is short and programmatic, that identification is stated, not analysed, and that it already contains both the decisive commitment (p. 16) and the acceptance of an addict made by another (n. 10), which the record's surveys date later. |
| [LIT-694](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-694.md) | Alternate Possibilities and Moral Responsibility | Frankfurt (1969), The Journal of Philosophy 66(23):829–839. The principle of alternate possibilities (PAP), "a person is morally responsible for what he has done only if he could have done otherwise", is false. Coercion excuses only when the agent acts because of it (§§II– III). Black, ready to make Jones4 act as he wants and never needing to, shows that circumstances can make an action unavoidable without playing any role in bringing it about (§IV); such a fact "does not help in any way to understand" the action and cannot excuse it (§V). PAP should be replaced by: not responsible "if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise", which "does not appear to conflict" with compatibilism (pp. 838–839). | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-546](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-546.md)); worth reading as the origin of Frankfurt-style cases and the shortest first-hand statement of the argument against the principle of alternate possibilities: a fact that makes an action unavoidable but plays no role in bringing it about cannot excuse, so PAP should give way to "a person is not morally responsible for what he has done if he did it only because he could not have done otherwise" (p. 838). Read it knowing that its case is schematic (Black, Jones4 and "a certain action"; the voting and shooting versions in the record's surveys are later retellings), that its prior sign is in a footnote, and that it leaves "could have done otherwise" and "morally responsible" unanalysed on purpose (n. 1). |
| [LIT-700](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-700.md) | Three kinds of collective attitudes | List (2014), Erkenntnis 79(S9):1601–1622. Collective attitudes come in three kinds. Aggregate attitudes summarise members' attitudes by a rule or a market, supervene proposition-wise and need not be rational. Common attitudes are held by all members with common awareness, matter for coordination, and inherit consistency from their unanimity. Corporate attitudes belong to a group agent, guide its action, supervene holistically on members' contributions and must be rational. The kinds are almost logically independent, and fears and hopes divide the same way as beliefs and desires. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-554](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-554.md)); worth reading as the disambiguation the collective-attitudes literature needs: aggregate attitudes (summaries, supervening proposition by proposition), common attitudes (unanimous and commonly known, supervening on a slightly enriched base) and corporate attitudes (a group agent's, supervening holistically and not straightforwardly reducible). The three are almost logically independent. A review by its own description, with no new theorem; its value for this record is that it names fears and hopes among the attitudes the split applies to, which gives the collective-emotion debate a vocabulary. |
| [LIT-705](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-705.md) | Group Agency and Supervenience | List & Pettit (2006), Southern Journal of Philosophy 44(S1):85–105. A group agent's rationality must supervene on its members' contributions, but not proposition by proposition. Three impossibility results show that robust group rationality (complete, consistent, deductively closed group judgments for every profile of rational member judgments) is inconsistent with majoritarian, uniform proposition-wise and proposition-wise supervenience. Premise-based and distributed premise-based procedures show it is consistent with set-wise supervenience, with group judgments that can be discontinuous with the members' judgments on the same proposition. Emergent agency without any member's conception of the group is set aside as unintelligible. | Active — read in full 2026-10-04 ([NOTE-550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-550.md)); worth reading as the short, formal core of List and Pettit's group agency: a group can be a robustly rational judge only if its judgment on a proposition is not, in general, a function of its members' judgments on that proposition. Group judgments supervene on members' judgments set-wise, not proposition-wise, so a group agent is individualistically unmysterious and still "not directly continuous" with its members. Read here as the lawful substitute for the unread book [LIT-391](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-391.md), whose chapter 3 takes up the same supervenience question; the impossibility results are cited from other papers, not proved here. |
| [LIT-707](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-707.md) | Aggregativity: Reductive Heuristics for Finding Emergence | Wimsatt (1997), Philosophy of Science 64(S4):S372–S384. Unread. Per its abstract: most scientists call a system property emergent if it depends on the parts' mode of organisation, a view consistent with reduction. Emergence is the failure of aggregativity, the state in which "the whole is nothing more than the sum of its parts". Aggregativity needs four conditions; met differently for different decompositions and in degrees, they give criteria for choosing decompositions and heuristics for detecting the biases of "vulgar reductionisms". | Deferred — filed 2026-10-04, not read: no lawful full text was reachable. Philosophy of Science's PSA supplement is paywalled at Cambridge Core and JSTOR, Unpaywall finds no open copy, and neither the 1997 paper nor its 2000 expansion is posted on Wimsatt's department pages. Content here is the publisher's abstract and Wimsatt's own summary in "Reductionism and its heuristics" (Synthese 2006), which his department posts and which was read in part. A person with library access could supply it; a reading would move this to Active and should state the four conditions exactly. |
| [LIT-713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-713.md) | Causation and Manipulability | Woodward, "Causation and Manipulability", Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy (2001; revised 2023). Causes are handles for manipulation: X causes Y iff some intervention on X, an exogenous change meeting conditions M1–M4 relative to Y, would change Y. The account is non-reductive but not viciously circular, needs no human agent, and distinguishes total, direct and contributing causes by combining interventions. Invariance and levels are not treated here. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-585](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-585.md)): in full, from the Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy's own open page (2023 revision). Worth reading as Woodward's compact statement of the interventionist account: X causes Y when an intervention on X, a surgical exogenous change defined by conditions M1–M4, would change Y. It answers the circularity and anthropocentrism objections and separates total, direct and contributing causes. Limits: it is a survey, and this version does not treat invariance, proportionality or levels of causation; for those the book ([LIT-723](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-723.md), unread) is needed. |
| [LIT-722](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-722.md) | Nonreductive Physicalism and the Limits of the Exclusion Principle | List & Menzies (2009), Journal of Philosophy 106:475–502. On a difference-making account of causation, Kim's exclusion principle is false. A revised principle (a property and its realizer never both cause the same effect) holds or fails system by system. The higher-level property is the cause, and excludes its realizer, exactly when the relation is realization-insensitive: the effect would still follow under nearby alternative realizations. | Active — read 2026-10-05 ([NOTE-560](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-560.md)): in full, from the authors' accepted manuscript on List's LSE page. Worth reading for a test of when a higher-level property is a cause in its own right. On a difference-making account, a higher-level property excludes its own realizer as the cause exactly when the effect would still follow had the property been realized differently (realization-insensitivity). Whether that holds is a fact about each causal system, not an a priori truth. Pernu ([LIT-147](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-147.md)) argues the neuroprosthetic example cannot carry it. |
| [LIT-723](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-723.md) | Making Things Happen: A Theory of Causal Explanation | Woodward (2003; Crossref print date 2004), Oxford University Press. A non-reductive, non-circular account of causation and explanation built on interventions; relationships that are stable under interventions are invariant, and invariance rather than lawhood explains causal explanation in the special sciences (per the publisher's abstract). Unread: the account of intervention is read in his SEP entry [LIT-713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-713.md); chapter 6 on invariance is not. | Deferred — registered 2026-10-05 from Crossref, not read: no lawful full text could be reached (the Oxford Academic page returned HTTP 403, and it is a subscription product). Its interventionist account is read first-hand in Woodward's Stanford Encyclopedia entry "Causation and Manipulability" ([LIT-713](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-713.md)). The entry does not treat invariance, so chapter 6, "Invariance" (pp. 239–314), is the part the owner's essay needs and has not read. It stays Deferred until a copy is supplied, not on merit. |
| [LIT-895](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-895.md) v2 | Moderate structural realism about space-time | Esfeld & Lam (2008), DOI-10.1007/s11229-006-9076-2, Synthese 160. Moderate structural realism accepts that relations require relata. It denies that the relata need intrinsic properties beyond their relations. Objects and relations are mutually dependent, with no priority either way, and relations supply identity conditions wherever intrinsic properties would. Where nothing discerns the relata (entangled quantum systems of one kind, points of a symmetric space-time), it takes numerical diversity as primitive, and denies that this is a thisness. In general relativity the relata are space-time points, not bare manifold points. They get a "structural identity" from the metric, or from a section of the orthonormal frame bundle. The hole argument counts against epistemic structural realism, and the question of what space-time relations relate counts against the radical version. The case is interpretive fit, not entailment. | Active — read in full 2026-10-10 ([NOTE-695](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-695.md)); worth reading as the founding statement of the no-priority, non-eliminative structural realism that Chakravartty's dilemma targets and that the owner's individuation thesis was placed beside. It says exactly what that position does with relata no relation discerns: entangled quantum systems of one kind and space-time points in symmetric space-times get a primitive numerical diversity, which the authors deny is a thisness or any kind of identity (pp. 33–34). The GR sections show that the tensor and fibre-bundle formulations fit the view, not that they require it. The one concrete construction of a point's "structural identity" they cite works only for space-times without symmetries, and it breaks the covariance the view rests on. |
